clinicalPearls: A neurodevelopmental disorder defined by persistent deficits in social communication and interaction together with restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests, or activities.
Symptoms are present from early development, though they may become fully apparent only when social demands exceed the child's capacities.
It is more frequently diagnosed in boys and shows a strong genetic contribution, with increased recurrence risk in siblings.
Early signs include reduced eye contact, limited joint attention and pointing, absent or delayed social smiling, and lack of response to name.
Repetitive behaviours may include hand-flapping, lining up objects, insistence on routines, and unusual sensory responses.
Diagnosis is clinical and based on developmental history and structured observation rather than a laboratory test.
Routine developmental surveillance and autism-specific screening in toddlerhood aid early identification.
Early intensive behavioural and educational intervention improves functional outcomes.
Common co-occurring conditions include intellectual disability, ADHD, anxiety, epilepsy, sleep problems, and gastrointestinal symptoms, and no evidence links vaccines to autism.
reference.pathophysiology: Autism arises from atypical early brain development influenced by a strong and heterogeneous genetic basis, including many single-gene syndromes, copy number variants, and polygenic risk, interacting with prenatal and perinatal factors. These influences alter neuronal connectivity, synaptic function, and the balance of excitation and inhibition during critical periods, affecting circuits underlying social cognition, language, and behavioural flexibility. No single mechanism or biomarker accounts for all cases, reflecting the disorder's biological heterogeneity.
additionalDifferentials: Global developmental delay or intellectual disability
Isolated language disorder or hearing impairment
Rett syndrome and other genetic or metabolic syndromes
Severe early deprivation or attachment disorder
additionalInvestigations: Formal audiology assessment to exclude hearing loss
Structured diagnostic observation and developmental history
Genetic evaluation (chromosomal microarray, fragile X testing, targeted panels)
Assessment of cognitive and adaptive functioning
Screening for co-occurring conditions such as epilepsy or sleep disorders
Metabolic testing when clinical features suggest an inborn error
redFlags: Regression or loss of previously acquired language or social skills
Absence of babbling, pointing, or other gestures by around 12 months
No single words by 16 months or no two-word phrases by 24 months
Seizures or focal neurological signs suggesting an underlying disorder
Concern for self-injurious behaviour or safety
reference.prognosis: Outcomes vary widely; language ability and cognitive level are important predictors, and early intervention improves adaptive functioning, though most individuals have lifelong needs requiring ongoing support.
pitfalls: Attributing early social and language concerns to shyness and delaying referral
Failing to test hearing before attributing delay to autism
Overlooking treatable co-occurring conditions such as epilepsy, anxiety, or sleep disturbance
Assuming intellectual ability from verbal fluency alone
management: Early structured behavioural and educational intervention (applied behavioural approaches, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy) as the mainstay to improve social communication and adaptive function
No pharmacotherapy for core features; antipsychotic agents such as risperidone or aripiprazole may be used for severe irritability or aggression
Identify and treat co-occurring conditions including epilepsy, sleep disorder, anxiety and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder
Family education, parent-mediated intervention and practical social support
Multidisciplinary paediatric, psychology, therapy and educational input with an individualised education plan
Genetic evaluation and counselling given the strong heritable contribution and increased sibling recurrence risk
Planning for transition to adult services and long-term support needs
